text:
(For the full report view the PDF available in the blue panel)

Foreword

Aviation continues to bring significant benefits to society, but it must do so while addressing its environmental and public health responsibilities.

Ultrafine particles (UFPs) are an area where scientific understanding is developing quickly, and where the sector has an important role to play in generating evidence and responding to what that evidence shows.

This White Paper sets out a view of what we know – and do not yet know – about UFPs in the aviation context. Its focus is understandably on emissions from aircraft engines, given the emerging scientific interest in combustion related UFPs, but it is also important to note that brake and tyre wear are additional sources of particulate emissions and merit further consideration as the evidence base develops.

The paper highlights the progress already made in improving air quality, the potential for further reductions through measures such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel, and the research now needed to understand exposure pathways and health implications more fully.

The Board welcomes Sustainable Aviation’s commitment to strengthening capability in UFP measurement and analysis, including its long-term investment in research. We strongly support this and look forward to Sustainable Aviation doing even more in the coming years to help the sector better understand and reduce UFP emissions.

Sustainable Aviation Advisory Board

The Sustainable Aviation Advisory Board works with Sustainable Aviation’s Council to provide independent advice and feedback.

Executive Summary

Sustainable Aviation (SA) is a coalition of UK airlines, airports, aerospace manufacturers, fuel producers and partners all committed to delivering net zero carbon aviation by 2050, and to minimising the aviation sector’s noise and air quality impacts.

For more than 20 years, Sustainable Aviation members have worked together to build a more sustainable future for our industry and ensure that aviation can continue to deliver substantial benefits to the UK and its economy.

Improving air quality around airports is a priority for SA and wider industry. We recognise that Ultrafine Particles (UFPs), defined as particulate matter with diameters less than 100 nanometers (PM0.1), have emerged as a pollutant of growing scientific interest, and that UFPs present unique challenges due to their small size, high number concentrations, and potential health impacts.

SA and its members remain committed to understanding and reducing these emissions through collaborative research, technological innovation, and policy engagement.

We first published a report on UK aviation and air quality in 2017. This concluded that aircraft emissions contribute 1% of the UK nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and 0.1% of UK particulate (PM10) emissions.

This White Paper provides the aviation industry’s current view on ambient local air quality, an overview of the recent research on UFPs, challenges facing the industry, and opportunities to further understand mitigation options for UFPs moving forward.

This paper sets out Sustainable Aviation’s position on UFPs. It reviews:

Current understanding of ambient air quality and UFPs in the aviation context.

Emerging research, including studies at Los Angeles International Airport and Boston Logan International Airport, which have found elevated concentrations of UFPs correlated with aviation.

Mitigation opportunities, such as the deployment of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF), hydrogen and electric aircraft and decarbonising airfield operations. SAFs have shown promise in reducing UFP emissions and improving air quality outcomes.

Research gaps, particularly in UFP measurement standardisation in the aviation context. SA is actively supporting research to close these gaps, including funding a PhD programme focused on UFP measurement at airports.

2. Air Quality

This section provides an overview of Sustainable Aviation’s previous publication on air quality and an update on our view of the current ambient air quality environment around airports.

2.1 Local Air Quality 2017 – 2025

The 2017 UK Aviation and Air Quality report explored the effect of UK aviation on local air quality and outlined the range of activities that were being undertaken throughout the industry to minimise emissions. This paper also considered emerging opportunities to further improve local air quality around airports/from aviation.

The findings in this paper describe the following elements that are still relevant to today’s operations:

Air emissions sources at and near to airports;

Air quality near to airports; monitoring, information sharing, air quality action plans;

Initiatives to reduce air quality emissions; and

Opportunities for improvement through collaboration.

In the eight years since the 2017 paper was published, concentrations of NO2, PM10 and PM2.5 in urban areas, including around UK airports, have been improving and are generally compliant with air quality standards.

More stringent air quality objectives for PM2.5 came into force in 2023 (DEFRA, 2023). These outline the air quality target values, long-term objectives and legally binding limit values for concentrations of major air pollutants that impact public health and ecosystems in the UK.

case study

Since 2017, air quality monitoring at Heathrow Airport shows a sustained improving trend in regulated pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide (NO2), PM10, and PM2.5. Current concentrations are below legally mandated limit values, reflecting the success of mitigation efforts such as cleaner ground operations, improved traffic management, and fleet modernisation.

This trend is mirrored at other major UK airports, where similar reductions in regulated emissions have been observed. These improvements are consistent with national air quality objectives and demonstrate the aviation sector’s commitment to reducing its environmental footprint.

As fleets continue to modernise with newer, cleaner aircraft and with increased uptake of SAF there is a strong likelihood that UFP emissions have already declined. However, due to the absence of consistent monitoring, these reductions have not been quantified. Such mitigation measures are discussed further in Section 4.

SA considers the existing 2017 paper a relevant reflection of the industry’s current local air quality position, as it relates to regulated air quality emissions.

The 2017 paper identifies UFP as an emerging scientific interest:

In addition to the pollutants discussed in the above, for which there is a strong and established evidence base, a smaller type of PM – ultra-fine particles (UFP) – are an emerging scientific interest. These particles are a sub-setof the emissions above.

Scientific research into UFP is still in its infancy, however Airports Council International has published a report (Airports Council International Europe, 2013) which provides an overview of available information on UFP and current understanding in an aviation context. This report was supported by airports that are members of Airport Council International. The report concludes that current understanding of average, long-term concentrations of UFP at airports, particularly in terms of dose effect is insufficient to establish any relationships. A review of studies of UFP concentrations shows that concentrations of UFP at airports are not notably higher than results from non-airport locations. Airports will continue to support further research in this area.

UK Aviation and Air Quality Report Sustainable Aviation, 2017 (page 49).

2.2 A focus on addressing UFPs

Since our Local Air Quality report was published, UFPs have become an area of intense interest with significant amounts of active research ongoing.

This paper addresses and reflects updated UFP research as our understanding of the relationship between UFPs and aviation develops.

To better understand the impacts of UFPs on air quality and the impacts of aviation on concentration patterns, we are engaging in and supporting targeted research in this field.

More detail on this can be found in Section 4.5.

3. Ultrafine Particles

This section provides an overview of Sustainable Aviation’s current understanding of the sources of ambient UFPs, their impacts on human health, regulatory limits and emerging research.

3.1 Sources of UFPs

UFPs are primarily emitted through combustion processes. According to the UK Government’s Air Quality Expert Group (Air Quality Expert Group, 2018), road vehicles are the major source of UFP emissions in the UK. However, there is growing scientific understanding that shows that exhaust emissions from aircraft engines include a relatively high concentration of UFPs. How these affect population areas, relative to other sources, is currently less well understood.

Studies, including those at Los Angeles International Airport (Dane Westerdahl, 2008) , Boston Logan International Airport (Chung et al., 2023) , and Barcelona-El Prat Airport (S. Ridolfo, 2024) , have found that elevated concentrations of UFPs are correlated with aircraft flight paths at longer-range distances from airport boundaries (about 10–15 km) compared to other aircraft emissions like NOx or PM, which are not

detectable at those distances. The Barcelona study also revealed significantly higher UFP concentrations within the airport, with aircraft operations, particularly taxiing and take-off, being major contributors. Historically, most concerns about UFPs at airports have been centred around occupational exposure, i.e. for those working on the airfield.

In 2014, Copenhagen Airport was required to set up a permanent UFP monitoring programme and “environmental” operating procedures to reduce aircraft emissions and UFP exposure (Stacey, 2019).

In March 2024, a court ruling mandated that the Dutch government must provide better protection for residents around Schiphol against UFPs and noise pollution (Schiphol, 2025).

Section 4 explores opportunities to reduce these emissions. However, as road vehicle emissions improve and shift to EVs, the proportion of UFP emissions from aviation will become greater.

As aviation’s relative contribution to UFP emissions grows, it is important to recognise the significant progress already made in reducing UFPs from other sources, particularly road transport. The removal of sulphur from petrol and diesel fuels has led to measurable improvements in urban air quality. Notably, research by the University of Birmingham (A.M. Jones, 2012) has shown a marked reduction in UFP concentrations at London Marylebone following these fuel specification changes. The study inferred that during the latter part of 2007 a 65% reduction occurred in the emissions of fine particles relative to NOx, from vehicles at Marylebone Road.

3.2 Impacts of UFPs on human health

We note that there is no consensus on health implications of UFPs (Stacey, 2019); however, a growing body of research suggests there may be health impacts. Like PM10 and PM2.5, UFPs have been associated with cardiovascular and respiratory health impacts. Due to their much smaller size, UFPs can penetrate more deeply into the lungs where they have been shown to enter the blood stream and end up in vital body organs, including the brain.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) global air quality guidelines (WHO, 2021) recognised that there is growing evidence of toxicology effects of UFPs, however, concluded that the evidence is not sufficient to formulate air quality guideline levels for exposure. The EU is also looking into new monitoring techniques.

The aviation industry is committed to the collection and monitoring of data that can be utilised by healthcare professionals for their assessment. SA members are working to ensure that data collected is comparable to other practitioners (please see Section 4.5).

Given the growing body of evidence linking aviation activity to elevated UFP concentrations and the potential health implications, a clear and coordinated approach is essential for addressing this.

As UFP emissions come from a wide range of sources (not just from aviation), we urge the UK Government to define a clear and coordinated path forward for addressing UFPs in the UK. This should include establishing a national framework for UFP monitoring, commissioning research into health impacts, and developing guidance for mitigation strategies. As road transport emissions decline, aviation’s relative contribution to UFPs will increase, making it essential that government policy keeps pace with emerging science and supports industry efforts to improve local air quality.

3.3 Regulatory limits for UFPs

Due to the lack of definitive health impact evidence, there is still no consensus on setting appropriate limit values for exposure to UFPs. The WHO published a “good practice statement” for UFPs (WHO, 2021), with thresholds associated with HIGH and LOW concentrations:

HIGH concentrations: 24-hour mean 10,000 particles/cm3 (24-hour

mean) or 1-hour mean > 20,000 particles/cm3

LOW concentrations: 24-hour mean <1,000 particles/cm3 (24-hour mean)

While these thresholds provide a useful framework for distinguishing between relatively clean and polluted environments, they are not currently realistic targets for most urban areas, where UFP levels routinely exceed the “high” threshold due to dense traffic, industrial activity, and other combustion sources. This highlights the need for context-sensitive approaches to UFP sources. This highlights the need for context-sensitive approaches to UFP management, including improved monitoring, targeted mitigation, and further research into health impacts and exposure pathways.

These thresholds are regularly exceeded across London (Stacey, 2022). Like PM10 and PM2.5, there is technically no health-based limit value below which exposure would be considered safe.

3.4 Emerging research

3.4.1 Emissions Measurement of UFP from Jet Engines

UFPs are hard to measure and require specialist tools to detect.

There is currently no established modelling methodology for environmental dispersion of UFPs, and monitoring of UFPs is not common practice, with only five long-term sites measuring UFP in the UK through Defra’s Particle Concentrations and Numbers Network (DEFRA, 2025).

Various studies have characterised UFP emissions, focusing on non volatile particles, using heated sampling systems. Direct measurement is made difficult due to high temperatures, complex mixing, and large exhaust volumes.

Findings from these studies are summarised below:

Particle Composition is predominantly carbonaceous.

Changing thrust settings will impact the size distribution of particles. This can be seen in the ICAO Emissions Data Bank (ICAO, 2025) where the average particle size changes at different thrust settings.

Different engine types produce varying particle sizes and compositions (ICAO, 2025).

While standardised measurement systems and regulatory limits for non volatile particles have been introduced for aircraft exhaust emissions through the ICAO CAEP 11 regulation, this does not capture the volatile particle emissions which also contribute to the total UFP composition at airports.

The ICAO regulation does not apply to Auxiliary Power Unit emissions, which are also a source of combustion.

3.4.2 Ambient Measurement of UFP at Airports

Studies conducted at various airports including Zurich, Copenhagen, Los Angeles, and Heathrow have identified the following findings:

The particle size distribution of UFPs near airports are smaller than those in urban environments.

Aircraft are recognised as a source of UFP, with higher concentrations

observed during takeoff and landing.

Elevated UFP levels near airports pose potential health risks.

3.4.3 Research Gaps and Future Directions

SA recognises the need for further research in the following areas:

Characterisation: Need for detailed studies on the size, composition, and behaviour of UFP as they disperse from the source, including the volatile component.

Standardisation: Harmonisation of ambient measurement techniques and calibration procedures to ensure data comparability for environmental dispersion.

Health Studies: More research needed to understand the health impacts of UFP exposure near airports.

Climate and atmospheric meteorology: As climate change increases the frequency of extreme heat events, atmospheric stagnation, and heat domes, further research is required to understand how these changing meteorological conditions affect UFP dispersion, secondary particle formation, and localised accumulation around airports.

4. Mitigation Opportunities and Actions

The aviation industry is implementing actions which should reduce UFP emissions. This includes the introduction of SAFs, which have a better air quality footprint than existing fossil fuels, making use of zero emission equipment as airport operations decarbonise, and further exploration of hydrogen and electric aircraft.

Hydrotreating conventional jet fuel also presents some opportunities, however, would require extensive testing. To help address knowledge gaps, SA is sponsoring further research into UFPs at airports.

4.1 Sustainable Aviation Fuel

SAFs, which reduce Greenhouse Gas emissions by 70% on an average lifecycle basis compared to Jet A-1 (Department for Transport, 2024), are one of the key mechanisms to decarbonisation in our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map (Sustainable Aviation, 2026).

There is increasing evidence of SAF reducing aviation’s non-CO2 impacts as well as potential for improving local air quality (R. S. Märkl, 2024).

The UK SAF Mandate, which was brought into effect 1 January 2025, and the Revenue Certainty Mechanism, will support a UK SAF production industry. The Mandate requires SAF to make up 2% of jet fuel blends in the UK in 2025, increasing linearly to 10% in 2030 and 22% in 2040.

SAF will be a prevalent focus for decarbonising aviation in the UK and globally. As SAF increases in jet fuel blends, we expect the respective air quality emissions of PM10 and PM2.5 to decrease.

In 2023, Virgin Atlantic led a consortium to deliver the world’s first flight across the Atlantic on 100% SAF to prove the safety of SAF and demonstrate its environmental benefits (Virgin Atlantic, 2024) . The SAF variant used in testing (88% HEFA-SPK, 12% Virent-SAK) used Synthesised Aromatic Kerosene to meet the current fuel specifications. These aromatic compounds are important to ensure compatibility with existing infrastructure but limit the nvPM benefit that can be achieved with low aromatic or zero aromatic SAF. nvPM are one aspect of UFPs.

The ECLIF3 project, involving UK and European partners, investigated the in-flight exhaust and contrail measurements of an Airbus A350 aircraft using 100% HEFA-SPK SAF with very low aromatics. This campaign showed a reduction in both nvPM and total PM at cruise conditions of 22-41%, dependent on the engine power level (Dischl et al., 2024).

Crucially, this reduction in nvPM emissions provides a dual climate and air quality benefit: by decreasing the number of soot particles that act as ice nucleation sites, low-aromatic SAFs reduce contrail ice crystal concentrations, thereby mitigating aviation’s non-CO2 climate warming impact (Märkl et al., 2024) alongside local UFP concentrations.

There are further research projects, ongoing, that are investigating the benefits of SAF such as PACIFIC which is investigating the impact of fuel composition and engine cycle on particle emissions, covering both local air quality and climate impacts using a range of techniques from laboratory tests to full-scale aircraft ground testing (Airbus, 2025).

Within the ICAO Committee on Aviation Environmental Protection (CAEP) work has been completed to develop guidance on predicting the impact that SAF usage has on aircraft engine exhaust emissions. This guidance will be published in an update to Doc 9889: Airport Air Quality Manual. The usage of SAF has a significant impact on both volatile and non-volatile particulate emissions. Because SAF contains virtually no sulphur, it directly eliminates fuel-derived gaseous SOx, thereby suppressing the nucleation of volatile ultrafine sulphate particles in the cooling exhaust plume. Simultaneously, the lower aromatic content of SAF reduces primary non-volatile particle (nvPM) formation during combustion.

For SOx emissions, due to SAF containing no sulphur, the reduction will be dependant solely on the blend ratio of SAF, i.e. a 50% reduction in SOx will be achieved when using a 50% SAF blend. The effect on nvPM mass and number is dependent on the fuel composition as well as the flight phase of the aircraft and the effect will vary for each aircraft/engine combination.

Typically, SAF contains a lower amount of aromatic compounds which results in a higher hydrogen content compared to Jet A-1 fuel leading to a reduction in the formation process of particles. The methodology of predicting non-volatile PM (nvPM) reduction through the use of SAF is therefore based on the change in hydrogen content. This method will be available in the update to the ICAO Airport Air Quality Manual and is also included in Appendix A.

The relationship between SAF and airport UFP levels is less well understood compared to that of SAF and aircraft nvPM emissions. This is one of the research gaps we are looking to address through measures outlined in Section 4.5.

4.2 Decarbonising airfield operations

The impact of reduced fuel burn on the airfield on UFP concentrations has not been modelled or understood. Measures to decarbonise airfields such as electrifying ground service equipment, fixed electrical ground power, pre-conditioned air, single engine taxi, and exploring hydrogen fuel for both aviation and ground support, will also have improvements on local air quality, including UFPs. Measures to reduce emissions from the landing and take-off cycle will also have an impact.

4.3 Hydrogen and electric aircraft

Our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map includes hydrogen and electric aircraft as part of the path to net zero. These technologies are areas of active research and development and will potentially provide benefits to LAQ once implemented as hydrogen powered aircraft, whether through combustion of hydrogen or hydrogen fuel cell, and electric aircraft will not produce any UFPs.

4.4 Hydrotreating conventional jet fuel

Improving conventional jet fuel quality alongside increasing levels of SAF is the most direct and scalable way the aviation industry can reduce UFP emissions. Conventional jet fuels can contain high aromatic and sulphur content due to the variable nature of global production.

One effective solution is hydrotreating, a refining process that removes aromatics and sulphur from jet fuel, resulting in lower particulate emissions. While a minimum level of aromatics is still required for compatibility with certain components, such as nitrile seals, fuel gauging systems and auto-ignition parameters, this constraint is less relevant for modern aircraft and fuel systems which are designed to operate safely with low-aromatic or aromatic-free fuels, though it should be noted that some SAFs may contain higher aromatic content than conventional jet.

However, any strategic recommendations regarding hydrotreating must carefully balance local air quality improvements against wider climate considerations. The additional processing required during hydrotreating increases refinery energy demand, which could impact upstream lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. Furthermore, reducing sulphur and aromatic content involves complex non-CO2 atmospheric trade-offs, including changes to aerosol radiative forcing. Consequently, the net climate impact must be fully evaluated alongside air quality benefits.

By phasing out legacy components and undertaking modifications with

associated costs to be compatible with low aromatics, the sector can unlock substantial air quality and climate benefits. As with the use of 100% SAF with low or zero aromatics, extensive testing will be required to ensure compatibility with existing aircraft as well as regulation and infrastructure changes before the full benefit of hydrotreating can be achieved.

4.5 Addressing research gaps

The measurement of UFPs and the impact of aviation on UFP concentration pathways and patterns is important to SA members. To address knowledge gaps on this topic, SA has sponsored a PhD student at the University of Birmingham. This PhD will run until 2031 and will address:

Measurement Technology

◦ Size range

◦ Suitability

◦ Calibration

◦ Co-location studies

Particle Characteristics

◦ Size from 0.5nm

◦ Composition of volatile and non-volatile fractions

◦ Behaviour of particles as they disperse downwind of exhaust

Impact on UFP levels from SAF

SA is supporting the PhD through funding, access to data and sites for data capture, and funding additional equipment as needed. Airport members are collaborating in a co-ordinated approach to support the PhD to give a view of the variety of airport locations and fleets across the UK.

4.5.1 Further Opportunities

The research outlined in Section 4.5 will deepen the industry’s understanding of UFP concentrations and dispersion patterns around airports. There is opportunity for regulatory standards to guide further measurement of UFPs across all known sources, including road which would greatly improve knowledge of UFP concentrations.

5. Summary

Sustainable Aviation is committed to understanding the impacts of UFPs and to mitigating risks to local air quality. This paper outlines our current understanding of UFPs, the potential opportunities to mitigate these impacts, and provides an overview of some of the work that the aviation industry is doing to mitigate these impacts and advance knowledge and understanding.

Crucially, while we actively support transparent evidence-gathering, policy frameworks must recognise that setting binding regulatory limits or operational mandates at this stage would be premature relative to the current state of science and technological maturity.

Sustainable Aviation will keep this topic under active review, continuing to support research that strengthens the evidence base so that any future policy or operational measures remain grounded in robust, validated science. As our understanding of UFPs improves, we will act to mitigate any outcomes accordingly.

As Canadian oil sands cutbacks squeeze conventional refiners, XCF Global demonstrates how domestic waste-to-fuel production insulates transportation fuel supplies from cross-border disruptions.

XCF Global Inc. (“XCF”) (NASDAQ:SAFX), a scaling U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (“SAF”), today addressed current dynamics across North American fuel markets as U.S. refiners face tighter crude slates following recent production pullbacks and maintenance across Canadian oil sands facilities.

Because Canadian heavy crude is a primary feedstock for North American diesel production, supply reductions create direct margin pressure and output bottlenecks for traditional refining infrastructure. XCF Global’s production model, anchored by its flagship New Rise Renewables Reno facility, operates entirely outside the petroleum crude supply chain, converting domestic agricultural and waste byproducts directly into drop-in distillates.

Key Strategic Advantages During Conventional Supply Squeezes:

Crude-Free Feedstock Independence: Unlike petroleum refiners tied to pipeline flows and heavy crude price spreads, XCF utilizes domestic waste streams (such as distillers corn oil) that are not impacted by geopolitical crude disruptions.

Drop-In Middle Distillate Relief: Renewable diesel functions as a direct, seamless replacement for petroleum diesel across commercial fleets, municipal transport, and industrial distribution without requiring engine modifications or new dispensing infrastructure.

Commercial Momentum: Building on its daily commercial delivery pace at the New Rise Reno facility, XCF continues to advance its operational throughput toward its permitted nameplate capacity of up to 38 million gallons per year.

“Whenever cross-border crude pipelines or oil sands extraction face downtime, conventional refiners feel an immediate squeeze in their middle distillate output,” said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. “XCF Global was built to solve this exact vulnerability. By refining domestic, waste-based feedstocks right here in the U.S., we deliver stable, commercial-scale renewable diesel while staying focused on scaling production where feedstock supply and customer demand are best aligned. That approach helps protect commercial fuel buyers from crude market shocks while supporting alternative lower emissions fuels.”

XCF believes its domestic, waste-based production model can support greater fuel supply resilience while providing a lower-carbon pathway for middle distillate production.

This will allow the technology company to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation of equipment for its cloud infrastructure.

text:
EVA Air, AIT Worldwide Logistics and Microsoft are launching a two-year program to use sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced from used cooking oil. In the first year, the project is expected to deliver around 15 thsd tons of CO₂ emissions reductions across Microsoft’s supply chain.

The SAF will be produced by Taiwan’s Formosa Petrochemical from used cooking oil. Both the feedstock and production process are certified under the ISCC system. According to the companies, the fuel can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.

EVA Air will provide Microsoft with SAF environmental attributes linked to flights departing Taiwan. This will allow the technology company to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation of equipment for its cloud infrastructure.

SAF use has already become part of EVA Air’s long-term strategy. The airline has been using sustainable aviation fuel on flights departing Asia, Europe and North America since 2025 and has also signed a five-year SAF procurement agreement with Formosa Petrochemical.

The expansion of SAF is creating additional demand for used vegetable oils, which are among the main feedstocks for producing this fuel through the HEFA pathway. Platts assessed SAF HEFA-SPK FOB Straits at $2,487.25 per ton on August 25, down $10 from the previous day.

text:
With increasing supply, ultra-low-carbon fuel will be a ‘game changer’

Propane, with its low carbon content and much lower harmful emissions than diesel and gasoline, has become a key tool for decarbonization and cleaner air around many of the United States’ more than 300 ports. From terminal tractors to up to Class 7 forklifts to generators and light- and medium-duty vehicles, propane-powered equipment is a good fit at both seaports and inland ports. Looking ahead to an even greener future, the next step in decarbonization for these key facilitators of American economic growth is renewable propane. As progress continues on ports’ path to zero carbon emissions, developments in renewable propane are poised to provide a big boost.

Renewable propane is molecularly identical to conventional propane, and is made from a variety of feedstocks, including camelina seed oil, vegetable oil, animal fats, and used cooking oil. It is a drop-in replacement for conventional propane, meaning customers can use renewable propane without additional infrastructure or costly new equipment.

That’s why propane providers like Jeff Stewart, president of Blue Star Gas in Santa Rosa, California, are bullish about renewable propane. Blue Star Gas is located in the state with two of the largest and busiest ports in America, the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach, and a state with aggressive goals for decarbonization. For Blue Star Gas’s customers, Stewart says renewable propane will be “a dramatic game changer” as supply continues to increase.

Increasing capacity of renewable propane

According to the U.S. Department of Energy Alternative Fuels Data Center, U.S. renewable propane production capacity is more than 4.5 million gallons per year. Stewart said that number is bound to increase, and perhaps significantly. The World Liquid Gas Association adds that renewable propane could meet half of the world’s propane demand by 2050. With propane distribution infrastructure already in place, it will be easy for ports of all sizes to adopt renewable propane.

“It’s not difficult to get renewable propane physically to a port,” he said. “It uses the same exact infrastructure as conventional propane. The challenge at this point is really in the volume and production. But we are starting to see new producers coming into the marketplace, and as the volume grows, there will be more supply available for ports.”

According to Stewart, renewable propane in the marketplace today is primarily a byproduct of the refining process for renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. While a good portion of renewable propane is generated at a refinery in Louisiana, refineries in California have recently become bio-refineries, and they aren’t using any crude-based feedstock.

Stewart reports that 20 percent of Blue Star’s volume is renewable propane Autogas — a form of propane used in vehicle applications and material handling. At the port, material handling remains the primary focus.

Progressing toward zero emissions with renewable propane

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Ports Initiative is an incentive-based program designed to reduce emissions by encouraging port authorities and terminal operators to retrofit and replace older diesel engines with new technologies and use cleaner fuels, such as conventional and renewable propane.

Renewable propane has a carbon intensity score of between 20 and 43. This compares to 80 for conventional propane and natural gas, both of which are 20% cleaner than gasoline and diesel (both 100). At 130, the average score of the U.S. electrical grid is the highest among all options.

Because renewable propane offers the same reliability and power as conventional propane, it can dramatically accelerate a port’s progress toward decarbonization while still being able to run efficient operations and meet tight deadlines for tasks like offloading ships.

For ports that want to step into the realm of renewable propane, which is typically blended with conventional propane, the process should be planned and calculated. That’s why Stewart said working with a propane provider with experience in renewable propane is a must.

“If you want to start a trial, that trial can be supported right now,” he said. “Depending on the volume and the eventual rollout, I think it will line up with the growth of the product.”

title: For the time being, biochar can be more cost-effective than sustainable aviation fuel.
description:
With sustainable aviation fuel, usually referred to as SAF in the industry, it is converted into a liquid fuel that replaces fossil kerosene.
What the comparison yields For biochar, the average comes out at approximately 177 dollars per ton of CO2.
For aviation fuel from residual and waste streams, that figure is around 448 dollars, so more than twice as high.
Clearly more expensive are the routes that produce aviation fuel from alcohol, at 938 dollars, and the route via rapid pyrolysis, at 652 dollars.
Those who sequester CO2 receive certificates at the project level, while those who supply fuel use aviation life cycle standards.
text:
Residual streams from forests, agriculture, and households now have numerous applications, ranging from green gas and heat to bio-based chemistry and materials. Two of these yield climate benefits in fundamentally different ways. With biochar, the material is heated without oxygen, resulting in a carbon-rich product that is applied to the soil, where the carbon remains for a long time instead of being released into the air as CO2. With sustainable aviation fuel, usually referred to as SAF in the industry, it is converted into a liquid fuel that replaces fossil kerosene. The first route removes carbon from the cycle; the second prevents the addition of new fossil carbon. It is precisely this difference that makes the two difficult to compare side by side.

Yet that is precisely what three researchers did in the open-access journal iScience, in an article published on August 21, 2026. Hassan El-Houjeiri of the KAPSARC research institute in Riyadh, Adam Brandt of Stanford University, and Mohammad Masnadi of the University of Pittsburgh deliberately focused on these two routes. Biomass is a scarce commodity with limitations regarding moisture content, energy density, and supply, they argue, and therefore its value is best realized in sectors where hardly any alternatives exist. Aviation is the prime example of this. Moreover, there are enough published cost studies on both routes to build a comparison. Other applications of residual streams fall outside their analysis.

What was missing until now was a way to make those studies comparable, the authors write. They converted everything to 2024 dollars and applied the same yardstick: what does it cost to remove one ton of CO2 from the air or keep it out? The research received no external funding, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.

What the comparison yields

For biochar, the average comes out at approximately 177 dollars per ton of CO2. For aviation fuel from residual and waste streams, that figure is around 448 dollars, so more than twice as high. For biochar, the most known cases range between 111 and 497 dollars. For SAF, the spread is much wider, from 98 to 948 dollars, and this is because very different techniques fall under that single umbrella.

These techniques are worth examining, as they differ significantly. The only route currently operating commercially on a large scale uses waste fats and oils and is called HEFA. This comes in at around 362 dollars per ton of CO2. Gasification followed by Fischer-Tropsch synthesis comes close to that at 342 dollars. Clearly more expensive are the routes that produce aviation fuel from alcohol, at 938 dollars, and the route via rapid pyrolysis, at 652 dollars. Precisely these more expensive routes are necessary to ever achieve large volumes, because there is simply not enough waste fat in the world. The researchers do note, however, that they could only find three and two public cases for those two, respectively—too few to base firm conclusions on.

The substantiation for biochar is more robust. The researchers used seventeen cost studies and also examined nineteen installations included in the Puro.earth certification register. Such installations are required to have verified how much CO2 they actually sequester, after deducting the emissions from collection and processing itself. This turned out to lie between 0,9 and 3,2 tonnes of CO2 per ton of biochar. Scale makes a significant difference here: an installation producing ten times as much does so at nearly sixty percent lower costs per ton. That gain has its limits, however, because beyond a certain scale, raw materials must be sourced from increasingly further afield. The researchers were unable to substantiate exactly where that tipping point lies with figures.

Not a choice, but an order

The main message of the study is not that biochar wins. The authors state in so many words that their outcome is not a prescription for where residual streams should go. That depends on what is available locally, who else lays claim to it, what subsidies are available, and what infrastructure is already in place. Moreover, they point out that biochar itself is part of a broader family of options for capturing carbon from biomass, and that some of these can prove cheaper or more sustainable in certain situations. Furthermore, the additional benefits of both routes, such as the soil activity of biochar or the contribution of SAF to one's own fuel supply, were not included in the cost comparison.

What the authors do point out is a difference in timing. Biochar is a mature technology that is already operational, accounting for an estimated global production capacity of more than 350 kilotons per year in 2023, spread across six continents. For the period up to approximately 2030, that is the route that can scale up rapidly. Aviation fuel from woody residues and household waste would only really start to matter in the 2030s and 2040s, and then only if the first factories of that type prove to operate reliably. That is not a given. The researchers point to a series of projects that were delayed, restructured, or failed altogether.

The current figures underscore how nascent that market still is. In 2025, around 2 million tonnes of SAF were produced worldwide, approximately 0,7 percent of all kerosene consumed by aircraft. In its forecast for 2050, aviation umbrella organization IATA assumes that waste fats and oils will supply slightly more than fifteen percent of SAF by then, agroforestry residues about a quarter, and household residual waste about seven percent.

For policymakers, there is another catch. Blending obligations, tax benefits, and purchasing agreements with airlines can push biomass towards fuel, even if sequestration per ton of CO2 is cheaper. Moreover, the two certification systems operate independently of each other. Those who sequester CO2 receive certificates at the project level, while those who supply fuel use aviation life cycle standards. As soon as the same raw material is listed in both systems, double counting is a real risk.

The researchers themselves call their study a snapshot and not a definitive ranking of biomass routes. Better operational data from SAF plants running on woody residues could still shift the picture.

text:
APPOINTMENT

Virgin Atlantic Appoints Sheeba George as Commercial Manager – India

Virgin Atlantic has appointed Sheeba George as Commercial Manager – India, effective October 1, 2026. She brings more than 25 years of aviation and commercial experience, including over 15 years with Virgin Atlantic.

In her new role, Sheeba will lead the airline’s commercial activities across India and work closely with customers and trade partners to deliver the India Country Sales Plan and support the airline’s growth in the market.

Sheeba has been with Virgin Atlantic since 2011 and most recently served as Regional Sales Manager – North India. Prior to this, she was Senior Account Manager, India, for more than 14 years.

Earlier in her career, she held Assistant Manager roles with United Airlines and Delta Air Lines, through GSA InterGlobe Air Transport, and began her aviation career with SAS – Scandinavian Airlines as a Sales Support Executive.

Her experience spans sales, business development, account management, forecasting, negotiation and sales planning across the Indian aviation market.

title: Metafuels, PSI open SAF demo plant in Switzerland to showcase aerobrew technology
description:
Metafuels and the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) have launched a demonstration plant in Villigen, Switzerland, to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from green hydrogen and CO₂.
The facility, known as “aerobrew,” will produce about 50 liters/day SAF and is designed to demonstrate the technology under industrially relevant conditions.
The process uses renewable electricity to produce hydrogen, which is combined with sustainably sourced CO₂ to produce green methanol.
Metafuels’ patented aerobrew technology then converts the methanol into synthetic kerosene.
PSI says the facility is the world’s first to integrate all methanol-to-SAF production steps at a single site.
text:
Metafuels and the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) have launched a demonstration plant in Villigen, Switzerland, to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from green hydrogen and CO₂. The facility, known as “aerobrew,” will produce about 50 liters/day SAF and is designed to demonstrate the technology under industrially relevant conditions.

The process uses renewable electricity to produce hydrogen, which is combined with sustainably sourced CO₂ to produce green methanol. Metafuels’ patented aerobrew technology then converts the methanol into synthetic kerosene. PSI says the facility is the world’s first to integrate all methanol-to-SAF production steps at a single site. Metafuels is targeting commercial-scale operations beginning in 2030.

title: Zero Petroleum eyes commercial plant after replicating Jet A-1 with green hydrogen
description:
UK start-up Zero Petroleum is working on its first commercial-scale plant after claiming to have proven the chemistry of a green hydrogen-based 100% replica of A-1 jet fuel.
It was produced at the firm’s pre-commercial Plant Zero.1 facility near Oxford, which features direct air capture equipment for CO2 sourcing, an electrolyser powered by solar energy for green hydrogen, and the company’s DirectFT synthesis platform.
Jet A-1 is particularly difficult to reproduce because it is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons to balance more than 70 chemical and physical properties, including density, freezing point, viscosity, thermal stability, and electrical characteristics.
Many SAF production methods make fuels that lack some of the components found in fossil jet fuel, meaning they may burn similarly but behave differently in aircraft fuel systems.
The company said testing by assurance firm Intertek confirmed the major properties of its synthetic fuel fell within the ranges found in conventional Jet A-1.
text:
UK start-up Zero Petroleum is working on its first commercial-scale plant after claiming to have proven the chemistry of a green hydrogen-based 100% replica of A-1 jet fuel.

The undisclosed facility recently had a pre-front-end engineering design (FEED) completed by Technip Energies and will produce a synthetic fuel Zero Petroleum claims could be used as the sole propellant for jet-engined aircraft.

According to the company, the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), created by combining green hydrogen and carbon dioxide (CO2) through Zero Petroleum’s Fischer-Tropsch synthesis process at its Oxford research facility, could eliminate the 50% blending limit applied to most SAF.

It was produced at the firm’s pre-commercial Plant Zero.1 facility near Oxford, which features direct air capture equipment for CO2 sourcing, an electrolyser powered by solar energy for green hydrogen, and the company’s DirectFT synthesis platform.

Jet A-1 is particularly difficult to reproduce because it is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons to balance more than 70 chemical and physical properties, including density, freezing point, viscosity, thermal stability, and electrical characteristics.

Many SAF production methods make fuels that lack some of the components found in fossil jet fuel, meaning they may burn similarly but behave differently in aircraft fuel systems.

The company said testing by assurance firm Intertek confirmed the major properties of its synthetic fuel fell within the ranges found in conventional Jet A-1.

Work on the fuel was backed by the UK SAF Clearing House, and the new facility’s pre-FEED benefitted from £3.5m ($4.1m) awarded through the Department for Transport’s (DFT) Advanced Fuels Fund grant.

While Zero Petroleum did not outline a timeline for the site’s construction, it said it is now “poised for commercial scale-up.”

It comes as the UK’s hydrogen aviation sector continues to garner steady public and private support as innovators strive to facilitate meeting UK SAF mandates dictating 10% of jet fuel supplied to the UK aviation market to be sustainable by 2030.

text:
Massive cargo ships that run on green methanol are now sailing scheduled routes, and ports and suppliers are organizing the infrastructure to fuel them.

In July, the world’s largest methanol dual-fuel container cargo ship, the 400-meter-long OOCL Wisdom, completed its first green methanol fueling (or “bunkering”) at China’s Qingdao Port. Days later, Dutch terminal operator VTTI completed its first large-scale green methanol bunkering load at its facility in Dalian, China. On 11 July, 20 organizations spanning shipping, ports, energy, and equipment manufacturing launched a Methanol Fuel Shipping Supply Chain Innovation Alliance to coordinate a national bunkering buildout.

Methanol fuel for shipping barely exists as an industry today. Yet if the global shipping fleet fully converts to methanol fuel, the industry’s annual methanol demand could reach 100 million tons a year by 2050, according to a National Center for Energy Analytics projection. That raises the question the industry has been dancing around for years—where is all that methanol supposed to come from?

For most of the previous century, making methanol meant building a colossal, centralized plant near a cheap natural-gas supply. A new wave of startups is betting that the old formula is backwards for the low-carbon methanol needed for shipping. Instead of piping stranded methane to a plant, the new idea holds, it’s cheaper to bring a plant to the methane.

Today, Emvolon—an MIT spinout founded in 2021 by Emmanuel Kasseris and Leslie Bromberg—announced the details of an agreement to sell up to US $450 million of the company’s biomethanol and other liquid fuels over a seven-year period to Stamford, Connecticut-based commodities trader Freepoint Commodities. Kasseris says the deal will fund construction of Emvolon’s fleet of modular, container-size plants, which convert methane from landfills and other waste sites directly into ship fuel.

Engine-Based Syngas Methanol Production

Rather than engineering a conventional chemical reformer, Emvolon repurposes an off-the-shelf automotive engine to help produce methanol. Emvolon runs the engine “fuel rich” (meaning more fuel is injected into the cylinders than can be burned with the amount of air in the mix). As a result, the cylinders produce syngas—a mix of carbon monoxide and hydrogen—instead of burning methane all the way to carbon dioxide and water. Syngas is then synthesized into methanol. Kasseris says the approach cuts the capital cost of small-scale chemical production by an order of magnitude compared with a purpose-built reformer.

Each complete system is roughly container-sized and converts about 3,500 cubic meters of methane into 8 tons of methanol a day. Trucked to a landfill, wastewater plant, or flare stack, it turns a gas stream that would otherwise be vented or burned into a liquid fuel that leaves by ordinary tanker truck—no new pipeline required.

A metal box that looks like an ordinary shipping container on the outside could contain machinery that converts the methane emitted by landfills and oil wells into green methanol. Emvolon

Emvolon has already moved from lab demonstration to commercial deployment. The company’s first commercial reformer is going up at a landfill in Humble, Texas, near Houston’s Bush Intercontinental Airport under a joint venture Emvolon and Montauk Renewables signed in 2025. The unit will run at roughly half a ton to a ton of methanol per day to start, Kasseris says, and Emvolon is targeting production to begin in 2027.

Emvolon isn’t limited to projects it develops itself. A landfill or gas-site owner could buy units outright and arrange separate offtake agreements for the produced methanol, Kasseris says. Emvolon can offer anything from equipment and training alone up to a full package of hardware, offtake, and financing—though he expects the company will eventually specialize in one side of that business as it scales.

A Growing Fleet of Methanol-Fueled Ships

Kasseris puts the current count of methanol-capable ships on order or in operation at roughly 400—evidence, in his view, of demand that’s already here. Ships calling at European ports already face the EU’s Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime rules, which price a vessel’s carbon intensity and push shipowners toward cleaner fuel. Kasseris expects Chinese policy to move the same direction; July’s alliance launch and the Maritime Technologies Forum‘s new methanol safety guidelines suggest the regulatory scaffolding is catching up to the hardware.

In addition to being environmentally friendly, green methanol scores points for practicality. It’s liquid at room temperature, easier to store than hydrogen or ammonia, and simpler to synthesize than long-chain synthetic hydrocarbons. Kasseris also notes that methanol isn’t a one-market bet; gasoline blending, industrial buyers, and eventually sustainable aviation fuel can all draw on the same supply.

The modular, at-the-source approach has been gaining adherents for years. WasteFuel, a Los Angeles-based waste-to-fuel developer, introduced a containerized “Methanol Module” in 2022 and has an offtake agreement with Maersk for 30,000 tons of bio-methanol annually. Maverick Synfuels, based in North Carolina’s Research Triangle, has marketed small, co-located gas-to-liquids plants since 2014. Houston-based HyOrc and engineering firm Re:Build Optimation are pursuing similar builds. WasteFuel, Maverick, and HyOrc did not respond to requests for comment from IEEE Spectrum.

text:
WOBURN, Mass. and STAMFORD, Conn., Aug. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Emvolon, Inc. (Emvolon), an MIT-spinout commercializing technology that converts methane-rich waste gases into high-value liquid fuels, and Freepoint Commodities LLC (Freepoint), a leading global physical commodity merchant, today announced the execution of two definitive commercial agreements. The transaction establishes Freepoint as both the anchor off-taker and a cornerstone project capital partner across Emvolon’s global deployment pipeline.

Under a seven-year Commodity Purchase Framework Agreement, Freepoint will serve as the primary buyer for biomethanol and associated liquid fuels produced across Emvolon’s deployment sites. Production volumes are structured to scale toward 300,000 metric tons annually as Emvolon’s portfolio expands, delivering commercial-scale fuel directly into Freepoint’s global physical distribution network.

In a concurrent financial agreement, Freepoint has secured direct co-investment participation rights to deploy equity and debt capital across Emvolon’s project portfolio and clean energy infrastructure assets. This balance-sheet backing bridges the gap between technology deployment and long-term project debt financing, providing waste asset operators, such as landfills, dairy farms, and industrial gas sites with a fully de-risked, turnkey fuel production solution.

“Energy security and supply chain resilience and sustainability dictate that we produce essential liquid fuels locally using domestic waste resources that are currently flared or lost,” said Emmanuel Kasseris, Ph.D., Co-Founder and CEO of Emvolon. “This dual commercial and capital agreement with Freepoint systematically solves the core bottleneck in decentralized fuel manufacturing by securing our buyer and anchoring our project financing platform. We are building our first commercial system now and will put that foundation to work across North America and key international growth regions.”

A Replicable "Fuels-as-a-Service" Blueprint for Global Expansion

Rather than operating as a passive technology licensor, Emvolon delivers a turnkey "Liquid Fuels-as-a-Service" platform that systematically eliminates execution risk for waste gas site owners. Emvolon’s commercial template aligns three essential pillars:

Site & Feedstock Development: Partnering with premier waste operators to secure stranded methane streams, as demonstrated by Emvolon's joint venture with Montauk Renewables.

Modular Conversion Technology: Deploying modular micro-reactors that repurpose mass-produced automotive engines to convert waste gas directly into liquid fuels on-site, bypassing grid and pipeline constraints.

Offtake, Logistics & Capital: Partnering with Freepoint to ensure product offtake, manage global distribution, and provide balance-sheet capital at the individual project level.

This standardized, plug-and-play template enables Emvolon to flexibly replicate projects across target regions, including landfill, agricultural, and industrial gas resource bases in North America and other regions, without custom engineering delays or regional infrastructure bottlenecks.

“Freepoint is focused on building resilient commodity supply chains and identifying proprietary technologies capable of scaling rapidly to meet physical supply deficits,” said Mark Lay, Managing Director at Freepoint. “Emvolon’s modular deployment model offers a practical solution to localized fuel production. Our dual commercial and capital commitment reflects our commitment to renewable chemicals and fuels.”

Capitalizing on Premium $1,000/Ton Commodity Demand

Methanol represents a $40 billion annual and rapidly-growing global market with diversified commercial applications across maritime shipping, heavy transport, specialty chemicals, and newly approved Methanol-to-Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) production pathways. Driven by global supply deficits for cost-competitive low-carbon fuels, RED-II-compliant biomethanol is trading at a premium exceeding $1,000 per metric ton. By producing low-cost liquid commodities directly at emission sites, Emvolon's modular economics deliver attractive commercial margins independent of shifting policy environments.

About Freepoint Commodities LLC

Founded in 2011, Freepoint is based in Stamford, Connecticut, and employs more than 600 people worldwide. The company is a global merchant of physical commodities, providing customers with physical supply and logistics chain management and services, along with environmentally friendly products and solutions. www.freepoint.com

About Emvolon, Inc.

Emvolon, Inc. is an MIT-spinout cleantech company founded in 2021 and headquartered in Woburn, Massachusetts. Emvolon’s patented technology platform converts waste gases from landfills, dairies, wastewater treatment facilities, and industrial flare gas into sustainable fuels and chemicals, including methanol, at the source of waste. The company serves hard-to-abate industries including maritime transportation, aviation, agriculture, energy, and waste management. www.emvolon.com

title: Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on $300 million renewable natural gas project
description:
Manure from one of Nebraska’s largest cattle-feeding operations will soon be used to produce renewable natural gas as Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on a $300 million project south of Broken Bow.
The renewable natural gas facility will use eight anaerobic digesters and is expected to produce about 1.2 million MMBtu of pipeline-quality renewable natural gas annually, according to the companies.
The gas will be processed to meet pipeline specifications, allowing it to be injected into existing natural gas infrastructure.

For Adams Land & Cattle, Babcock said the renewable energy project also creates possibilities for a more integrated cattle-feeding operation.
text:
Manure from one of Nebraska’s largest cattle-feeding operations will soon be used to produce renewable natural gas as Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on a $300 million project south of Broken Bow.

The Broken Bow-based cattle feeder is partnering with Neogenyx Fuels to build an anaerobic digestion facility that will convert cattle manure into pipeline-quality renewable natural gas.

Adams Land & Cattle CEO Abram Babcock said the project represents a new way to capture value from a byproduct the feedlot has long had to manage.

“It’s something we’ve had to manage. It’s a byproduct,” Babcock said in an interview. “We can extract and capture the gas and generate revenue.”

The project is being built alongside a major renovation of the Adams feedlot, including the use of roller-compacted concrete.

The renewable natural gas facility will use eight anaerobic digesters and is expected to produce about 1.2 million MMBtu of pipeline-quality renewable natural gas annually, according to the companies. It is expected to avoid up to 63,700 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year.

The gas will be processed to meet pipeline specifications, allowing it to be injected into existing natural gas infrastructure.

Mike Bakas, CEO of Neogenyx Fuels, said that creates potential markets well beyond Nebraska, including the international maritime industry.

“This product is essentially, when we’re done, the same constituency of natural gas,” Bakas said. “We have to meet a specification set by the pipeline company to be able to inject our gas into the pipeline.”

Bakas said renewable natural gas produced from the cattle manure could eventually be converted to liquefied natural gas for use as a lower-carbon marine fuel.

The project also is designed to recover additional products from the manure.

A screw press will separate a fibrous material that Adams plans to use for cattle bedding. A centrifuge will separate nutrients into concentrated phosphorus and nitrogen fertilizer products.

Babcock said the process will allow the operation to retain the phosphorus and nitrogen that are valuable to farmers while producing a more concentrated fertilizer product.

Neogenyx also expects to capture biogenic carbon dioxide from the process. Bakas said that nearly pure stream of carbon dioxide could potentially be used for industrial purposes or, with additional processing, beverage-grade applications.

The companies describe the project as an early example of pairing a large cattle-feeding operation with renewable fuel production.

“This is a way that we can continue to leverage rural America to help with that production,” Babcock said.

Babcock said the project represents a significant investment in Broken Bow and Custer County. He said the partnership is expected to continue for at least 25 years.

The project is also expected to create more than 100 construction jobs and about 20 permanent operational jobs, according to Neogenyx.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, who attended the groundbreaking, called it a major day for Broken Bow and Nebraska agriculture.

“Nebraska’s growing some food, and now we’re energy,” Pillen said.

U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts said the project demonstrates how agricultural waste can become part of the nation’s energy supply.

“Agriculture is the heart of what we do, and we want to create more value added agriculture. And this project brings together two key ones livestock and biofuels. And by taking the manure off the cattle and turning it into renewable natural gas, we’re adding to American energy dominance. We’re making it so we bring our energy prices down,” Ricketts said in an interview.

Ricketts said renewable natural gas adds another value-added opportunity for Nebraska agriculture, alongside ethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel and the developing sustainable aviation fuel industry.

For Adams Land & Cattle, Babcock said the renewable energy project also creates possibilities for a more integrated cattle-feeding operation.

“We just have a lot of opportunities,” he said.

The renewable natural gas facility is Neogenyx Fuels’ first agricultural anaerobic digester project. The company will own and operate the facility, while Adams Land & Cattle will provide the manure and handle the nutrient products produced by the process.

The companies expect the facility to demonstrate how livestock agriculture can participate in emerging energy markets while creating new revenue streams in rural communities.

text:
As Canadian oil sands cutbacks squeeze conventional refiners, XCF Global demonstrates how domestic waste-to-fuel production insulates transportation fuel supplies from cross-border disruptions.

XCF Global Inc. ("XCF") (NASDAQ: SAFX), a scaling U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel ("SAF"), today addressed current dynamics across North American fuel markets as U.S. refiners face tighter crude slates following recent production pullbacks and maintenance across Canadian oil sands facilities.

Because Canadian heavy crude is a primary feedstock for North American diesel production, supply reductions create direct margin pressure and output bottlenecks for traditional refining infrastructure. XCF Global's production model, anchored by its flagship New Rise Renewables Reno facility, operates entirely outside the petroleum crude supply chain, converting domestic agricultural and waste byproducts directly into drop-in distillates.

Key Strategic Advantages During Conventional Supply Squeezes:

Crude-Free Feedstock Independence: Unlike petroleum refiners tied to pipeline flows and heavy crude price spreads, XCF utilizes domestic waste streams (such as distillers corn oil) that are not impacted by geopolitical crude disruptions.

Drop-In Middle Distillate Relief: Renewable diesel functions as a direct, seamless replacement for petroleum diesel across commercial fleets, municipal transport, and industrial distribution without requiring engine modifications or new dispensing infrastructure.

Commercial Momentum: Building on its daily commercial delivery pace at the New Rise Reno facility, XCF continues to advance its operational throughput toward its permitted nameplate capacity of up to 38 million gallons per year.

"Whenever cross-border crude pipelines or oil sands extraction face downtime, conventional refiners feel an immediate squeeze in their middle distillate output," said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. "XCF Global was built to solve this exact vulnerability. By refining domestic, waste-based feedstocks right here in the U.S., we deliver stable, commercial-scale renewable diesel while staying focused on scaling production where feedstock supply and customer demand are best aligned. That approach helps protect commercial fuel buyers from crude market shocks while supporting alternative lower emissions fuels."

XCF believes its domestic, waste-based production model can support greater fuel supply resilience while providing a lower-carbon pathway for middle distillate production.

About XCF Global, Inc.

XCF Global, Inc. ("XCF") is a U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel ("SAF") focused on decarbonizing transportation while supporting domestic fuel supply and energy security. The Company's flagship facility, New Rise Renewables Reno, has a permitted nameplate production capacity of up to 38 million gallons per year. XCF intends to advance a pipeline of potential expansion opportunities in Nevada, North Carolina and Florida and to build relationships across the energy and transportation sectors that it believes could support the scaling of renewable fuels production. Any such opportunities remain subject to, among other factors, feasibility assessments, financing, regulatory approvals and market conditions. XCF is listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market and trades under the symbol SAFX.

text:
The Aussie startup turning forest offcuts into jet fuel ✈️

HAMR Energy just secured up to $32 million from ARENA to build Australia’s first large-scale methanol-to-jet refinery, in Port Adelaide 👇

🌲 The feedstock. Harvest a plantation forest and the branches, the offcuts, the bits the timber mill can’t use get left on the ground. HAMR takes that.

⚡ The process. Renewable electricity and hydrogen turn the waste wood into methanol first, then into sustainable aviation fuel.

📊 The scale. At full size the projects are built to take 600,000 tonnes of forestry residue a year and turn it into around 140 million litres of aviation fuel. HAMR estimates about 85% lower emissions than fossil fuels.

💰 The money. Up to $32 million, staged. $12.5 million now, $19.5 million once co-funding lands. First project backed under the government’s $250 million low carbon liquid fuels priority.

🏗 The founders. Engineers Alex Smith and David Stribley started HAMR in Melbourne in 2020. Stribley says it leads to the first fuel refinery built in Australia in 40 years.

Aviation is one of the hardest things on earth to run without fossil fuel. So part of the answer might be the wood we’ve been leaving to rot 🤝

text:
Strengthening Commitment to Sustainable Aviation

EVA Air, in collaboration with the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) and Microsoft, has announced an expansion of its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) initiative, reinforcing efforts to reduce the carbon footprint of air transportation. This partnership will see flights departing from Taiwan utilizing SAF supplied by Formosa Petrochemical Corporation (FPCC). The fuel is derived from used cooking oil (UCO) and certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) system, which ensures that both the feedstock and production processes adhere to stringent sustainability criteria.

Clay Sun, President of EVA Air, emphasized the importance of cross-sector collaboration in achieving net-zero aviation. He noted that aligning customer demand with industry capabilities can accelerate the development of the SAF market, and expressed optimism about expanding partnerships to establish lower-carbon air transportation as a global supply chain standard.

Environmental Impact and Corporate Responsibility

Sustainable aviation fuel offers a significant environmental advantage, reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 80% compared to conventional jet fuel. The environmental benefits of the SAF used in this initiative will be tracked and retired through the ISCC Credit Transfer System (CTS), an internationally recognized registry that monitors sustainability attributes. This mechanism allows Microsoft to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with its air freight operations, reflecting a broader corporate trend toward addressing indirect emissions within supply chains.

Microsoft’s participation is expected to stimulate increased corporate demand for SAF, potentially encouraging wider adoption across the aviation industry and further emissions reductions. As companies intensify efforts to lower their carbon footprints, investor interest in sustainable aviation initiatives is likely to grow. This dynamic may prompt competitors to enhance their own SAF strategies or pursue similar partnerships to maintain market relevance.

Challenges and Future Outlook

Despite the positive momentum, the expansion of sustainable aviation fuel faces notable challenges. High initial production costs, logistical complexities in scaling supply, and the need to navigate regulatory frameworks across different jurisdictions remain significant obstacles. Overcoming these issues will require sustained cooperation among airlines, fuel producers, policymakers, and corporate customers.

The partnership between EVA Air, AIT, and Microsoft underscores both the potential and the difficulties inherent in transitioning to sustainable aviation. By aligning customer demand with industry resources, the initiative seeks to establish a new benchmark for lower-carbon air transportation within global supply chains.

Burckhardt Compression has secured two orders for the Boaventura Energy Complex, a major Petrobras project in Brazil, for the supply of six PL2 compressor packages and related services. The orders mark an important milestone in the company's strategy to expand its presence in South America's growing energy market.

The compressor packages were ordered by Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) companies responsible for executing three parallel projects within the Boaventura Energy Complex in Itaboraí, Rio de Janeiro. It demonstrates the value of being close to our customers, understanding their needs and supporting them with local expertise backed by global engineering capabilities."

The contract reflects Burckhardt Compression's increased focus on South America and the close collaboration established with Petrobras and its project partners in recent years. Supported by its recently opened additional service center in Brazil, the company continues to strengthen its local presence and service capabilities across the region.

text:
KROHNE has been highlighting its process instrumentation portfolio engineered for the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market.

The portfolio enables producers to manage challenging feedstocks, hydrogen service and demanding process conditions ranging from pretreatment through the final downstream process.

As SAF projects move from first-of-a-kind plants toward larger-scale deployment, engineers are under pressure to upscale the process while maintaining reliable, economically viable production assets.

“The SAF industry brings together two very different worlds,” said Yannick Farine, industry manager biofuels and bioenergy at KROHNE.

“Success depends on understanding the behavior of renewable feedstocks upstream while also meeting the demands of downstream refining. Our goal is to help customers optimise processes, reduce maintenance and build SAF plants they can rely on for years to come.”

A central element of this concept is the wider use of ultrasonic flowmeters in SAF service. Unlike many traditional technologies, ultrasonic flowmeters have no internal restrictions, capillaries or moving parts and are well suited to abrasive feedstocks, hydrogen-rich streams, high-pressure steam and other critical services.

Their ability to operate at temperatures up to 600C and at high pressures for both liquids and gases makes them one of the few technologies capable of delivering accurate measurement across a broad envelope of SAF conditions.

Advanced noise-filtering in ultrasonic gas flowmeters also supports reliable hydrogen measurement, which can be challenging due to the gas’s high velocity of sound and demanding operating environment.

text:
Global law firm Clifford Chance has advised the lenders on the financing of Egypt's first sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production facility.

The project marks the development of the first project-financed SAF plant in Africa and the Middle East.

The $212.4 million (£181 million) project is supported by a $142.9 million (£122 million) debt package provided by The Arab Energy Fund (TAEF), Qatar National Bank (QNB) and The Emerging Africa & Asia Infrastructure Fund and Emerging Markets Transition Debt Fund, funds managed by Ninety One.

Shell will act as the plant's primary feedstock provider and sole offtaker, pursuant to a long-term take-or-pay offtake agreement, supporting the project's long-term commercial viability. Axens will provide its proprietary processing technology.

Located in the Sokhna Special Economic Zone in Egypt, the project is being developed with the support of sponsors Green Sky Capital Management, Al Mana Holding and Vision Invest.

The facility is designed to produce 200,000 tonnes per annum of biofuels, including SAF and other green products and will utilise Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) technology to convert waste-based feedstock into high-grade sustainable fuel.
